metadata.title: Learning What the Crowd Would Say.
metadata.clock: narration (Kokoro af_bella) — per-beat mp3 durations are MEASURED, never estimated
metadata.greeting_note: hello lexicon: Italian (Ciao) — one of the short forms the HAI persona's word budget allows. Rotated off Ep. 03's 'Hej' so no two episodes in the series repeat a language.
metadata.purpose: Ep. 04 of the AI in Astronomy & Space Science series, built from weekly_stem_videos/ideas.md Astronomy topic 04 (Galaxy classification at scale — Galaxy Zoo + CNNs sorting millions of galaxy images by shape). Per the series notes in ideas.md, Ep. 01 already established the data-volume premise, so this episode skips the 'too much data' framing entirely and goes straight to the mechanism.
metadata.color_semantics: Claude fidelity palette. Terracotta #D97757 is the ONE accent and marks exactly one focal event per beat: the vote fraction, the rotation, the uncertain galaxy, the survey the model was NOT trained on. Galaxy cutouts are dark tiles on the cream ground — the way plates are printed in a paper — and never carry the accent.
metadata.distinct_from_ep03: Ep. 03 (gravitational-wave detection) landed on out-of-distribution failure: a classifier cannot name a class it has never seen. Ep. 04 deliberately does NOT repeat that. Its idea is that the LABEL ITSELF is a distribution — a vote fraction — and its limit is that the model's ceiling is the crowd's judgement plus the survey it was trained on. Galaxy Zoo's serendipitous volunteer discoveries (Hanny's Voorwerp, Green Peas) were verified and then deliberately left out, because that beat would have been Ep. 03's punchline a second time. See FACTCHECK.md.
metadata.note: ILLUSTRATE LAW: the Claude UI appears at B00 (cold open, with RESULT lines), B11 (verdict artifact), B12 (handoff), B13 (title outro). Every other beat illustrates its concept as a reel-local Manim scene (scenes.py) in the Claude fidelity palette. Galaxy imagery is SYNTHETIC and generated by assets/gen_galaxies.py — deterministic, seeded, captioned as synthetic wherever a viewer could mistake it for data. No LaTeX/MathTex anywhere. metadata.channel_title is omitted for the same GATE V edge-bleed reason logged in Ep. 03's BUILD-LOG.

beats.narration_text: Sorting galaxies by shape used to be a job you did by eye, one at a time. Here is how that became a machine that measures millions of them, and what it can and cannot tell you.

show.event: cream page; IRREDUCIBLY HUMAN eyebrow, then the serif segment title Learning What the Crowd Would Say
spark + greeting Ciao, HAI settles above the composer card
the ask types itself into the composer; send button arms when it lands
terracotta running indicator: counting the votes…
three result lines stagger in — method, accuracy, limit. The ask lands ANSWERED.

props.segment: Learning What the Crowd Would Say
props.command: Galaxy Zoo asked the public to sort galaxies by shape, and there are now catalogues of millions of them. What is the actual method, how accurate is it, and where does it break?
output: method — a CNN trained to predict human vote fractions
accuracy — ~99% on confident answers; fractions within 5-10%
limit — it predicts the crowd, and it does not travel between surveys

beats.narration_text: I am Om Mali, and this is Humanitarians AI. This one is about a method that does something slightly strange. It does not learn what a galaxy is. It learns what people would say about it.

show.event: top-left kicker: AI IN ASTRONOMY & SPACE SCIENCE · EP. 04
the name OM MALI draws on large, centre-left, terracotta hairline sweeping under it
role line fades in beneath: Humanitarians AI · presenter
the claim sets on the right: 'It does not learn what a galaxy is' struck through, then 'It learns what people would say about it' in the accented token
@HumanitariansAI wordmark bug settles bottom-right, inside title-safe

beats.narration_text: Here is the whole idea in one breath. A galaxy's shape is a clue to its history, but shape is a judgement call. So astronomers asked hundreds of thousands of people to make that call, kept the disagreement instead of hiding it, and trained a network to predict the disagreement.

show.event: eyebrow: THE WHOLE IDEA, IN ONE BREATH
line 1 sets: 'shape is a clue' — a single synthetic galaxy cutout appears left
line 2 sets: 'but shape is a judgement call' — a spread of tally marks fans out beside the cutout, not one answer but many
line 3 sets: 'keep the disagreement' — the tallies resolve into a small bar of proportions rather than a single label
the closing line lands: PREDICT THE DISAGREEMENT, terracotta rule under it

beats.narration_text: Start with what is being sorted. Smooth and featureless. A disc with spiral arms. A bar cutting through the middle. A disc seen edge on, with a dust lane. Two galaxies mid collision. Shape carries the history, which is why anybody bothers to label it.

show.event: title: WHAT IS BEING SORTED; five empty framed tiles draw across the stage
tile 1 fills with a smooth elliptical, label SMOOTH lands under it on the spoken word
tile 2 fills with a two-arm spiral, label SPIRAL
tile 3 fills with a barred spiral, label BARRED, and the bar is ringed in terracotta
tile 4 fills with an edge-on disc, label EDGE ON
tile 5 fills with a merger, label MERGER
footer: shape encodes formation history · synthetic cutouts, generated for this episode

beats.narration_text: July 2007. Galaxy Zoo puts about nine hundred thousand telescope images online and asks the public to sort them. Within twelve hours it is taking twenty thousand classifications an hour. But the design decision that matters is not the crowd. It is that every galaxy gets looked at by many people.

show.event: title: GALAXY ZOO · 11 JULY 2007; a dense synthetic survey field fills the left of the stage
counter climbs to 900,000 galaxies, cited Lintott et al. 2011
a rate line ticks up to 20,000 classifications per hour with the caption 'within twelve hours'
right side: ONE galaxy tile is lifted out of the field and a row of small human marks accumulates beneath it
the marks reach an average of 38 per galaxy, in terracotta — the beat's one accent
closing line: the point is not the crowd, it is the repeat looks

beats.narration_text: And they are not asked for a name. They are walked down a decision tree. Is it smooth, or does it have features? If it has features, is there a bar? How many arms? Eleven questions, and your answer decides which one you get next.

show.event: title: NOT A NAME, A PATH; the hero galaxy tile sits left
the root question draws: 'smooth, or features?' with two answer nodes
the FEATURES branch lights and a second question opens beneath it: 'is there a bar?'
a third question opens: 'how many arms?' — the tree is now three levels deep
the traversed path is drawn in terracotta from root to leaf; the untaken branches stay ink at reduced weight
footer: 11 tasks in the GZ2 tree, 2 to 7 answers each · Willett et al. 2013

beats.narration_text: So here is the method. One galaxy, one tree, many people. Their answers become a vote fraction, the share who chose each option. A convolutional network trains to predict that fraction. And then active learning closes the loop, sending back to the volunteers only the galaxies the network is unsure about.

show.event: title: THE LOOP; four numbered stations draw left to right as empty cards
station 1 lights: ASK — a galaxy tile plus the decision tree glyph
station 2 lights: TALLY — many marks collapse into a proportion bar, not a single label
station 3 lights: TRAIN — the proportion bar feeds a layered network glyph
station 4 lights: PREDICT — the network emits a fraction for an unseen galaxy
a terracotta return arc closes the loop from station 4 back to station 1, captioned 'active learning: only the galaxies it is unsure about'

beats.narration_text: Run one galaxy through it. This one has a bar, but a faint one. Say sixty three of a hundred people call it barred and thirty seven do not. The training target is not the word bar. It is zero point six three, and the network learns to land on that number.

show.event: the four stations persist as a thin rail across the top; the hero galaxy sits large on the left with its bar ringed
a 10x10 grid of small human marks fills in; 63 of them tip to the BAR side, 37 to NO BAR
the grid collapses into a proportion bar reading 0.63 / 0.37
a struck-through card shows what is NOT the target: the single word 'barred'
the real target lands in terracotta: 0.63
the network glyph returns its prediction beside it, and the caption marks the split as illustrative

beats.narration_text: Now the design decision that makes it work. A galaxy has no up. Rotate the image and the answer must not change. So the winning architecture from the twenty fourteen competition fed the same galaxy in at several orientations, through shared weights. The physics told the network what to ignore.

show.event: title: A GALAXY HAS NO UP; one spiral cutout centre-left
four copies fan out, each rotated — 0, 45, 90, 135 degrees — and the label under each stays identical
arrows from all four converge on a single shared-weights block, drawn once and reused
the shared block is ringed in terracotta and captioned 'same weights, four views'
closing line: the physics tells the network what to ignore
footer cite: Dieleman, Willett & Dambre 2015 · Galaxy Challenge 2014

beats.narration_text: The numbers. Against confident volunteer answers the trained networks are about ninety nine percent accurate on every question, and they predict the vote fractions to within five to ten percent. The current catalogue covers eight point six seven million galaxies.

show.event: title: WHAT IT ACTUALLY DELIVERS
left: an accuracy arc fills to ~99% on confident volunteer answers, cited Walmsley et al. 2022
centre: a predicted-vs-actual fraction plot, the predicted points landing inside a terracotta band marked 5-10%
right: the counter runs to 8,670,000 galaxies, cited Galaxy Zoo DESI
a forward marker notes what is coming: Rubin's ten-year survey, about 20 billion galaxies

beats.narration_text: Now decide whether you should use this. It predicts people. Its ceiling is what the crowd would say, so where the crowd is wrong, it is confidently wrong with them. And it does not travel. A network trained on one survey's images cannot be dropped onto another telescope's, because the pixels shift underneath it.

show.event: title: TWO CEILINGS; the stage splits into two panels
left panel: the crowd's answer and the model's answer sit on the same line, and a TRUTH marker sits somewhere else entirely
the gap between them is bracketed in terracotta and labelled 'the model cannot be more right than the crowd'
right panel: the same galaxy rendered as two survey cutouts with different depth and pixel scale, side by side
an arrow from survey A's trained network to survey B's image is struck through; caption 'distributional mismatch'
footer cite: Walmsley et al. 2022 · domain-shift result, arXiv 2412.15533

beats.narration_text: Let's recap with Claude. The label is a distribution, not a word. The method is a decision tree, many humans, and a network trained on the vote fractions. The result is about ninety nine percent on confident answers across nearly nine million galaxies. And the limit is that it predicts people, not truth.

show.event: the artifact page scales up on the cream stage, spark + title bar
four numbered recap lines stagger in, one per spoken clause

props.artifactTitle: Learning What the Crowd Would Say — one page
artifactLines: The label is a distribution, not a word: the target is the fraction of humans who chose each answer.
The method: an 11-question decision tree, many volunteers per galaxy, a CNN trained on the vote fractions.
The design tell: a galaxy has no up, so the same image is fed in at several orientations through shared weights.
The limit: its ceiling is the crowd, and a network trained on one survey does not transfer to another.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this one. I have a labelling task where expert annotators genuinely disagree. Show me how to keep the disagreement as a soft label instead of forcing a majority vote, pick a loss and a calibration check for predicting label distributions, and design an active learning rule that sends only the informative examples back to humans. Then grade the answer on three things. Does it name a loss. Does it check calibration, not just accuracy. And does it say when to stop asking people.

show.event: spark + greeting 'Your turn.' — the one greeting that drops the persona
the suggested prompt types itself into the composer while the voice reads it verbatim
terracotta running line: paste this into Claude…
the three-item rubric staggers in as output lines, one per spoken grading criterion
